stem: The elements in the third period, and their compounds, show trends in their physical and chemical properties.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
A sketch graph of the first ionisation energies of five successive elements in the third period is shown.

{{figure:pdf_visual_01.png}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Explain why there is a general increase in the first ionisation energy across the third period.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Sketch, on the graph, the position of the ionisation energies of the two elements that come before $\text{Mg}$ in this sequence.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Explain, with reference to electron arrangements, the decreases in first ionisation energy between $\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Al}$ and between $\text{P}$ and $\text{S}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.stem:
The chlorides of the elements in the third period behave in different ways when added to water, depending on their structure and bonding.

$\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{M}$ are each a chloride of an element in Period 3. A student investigated $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{M}$ and their results are given.

$\mathbf{L}$ is a white crystalline solid with a melting point of $987\text{ K}$. $\mathbf{L}$ dissolves in water to form an approximately neutral solution. Addition of $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to an aqueous solution of $\mathbf{L}$ produces a white precipitate.

$\mathbf{M}$ is a liquid with a boiling point of $331\text{ K}$. $\mathbf{M}$ is hydrolysed rapidly by cold water to form a strongly acidic solution, a white solid and white fumes.

Identify $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{M}$.
Explain any properties and observations described.
Give equations where appropriate.
